newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Punt seen weaker as sterling forges ahead - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Punt seen weaker as sterling forges ahead - analysts.

text.p: The Irish pound languished below 98 pence on Friday as on-going sterling strength and mark malaise depressed the punt against the British currency while keeping it firmly pinned at the top of the ERM grid.

The punt's fate hinges on sterling/mark's progress and analysts see no let-up in the British currency's upward march against the mark given the very different interest rate outlooks in the two countries.
A further rise in UK rates is widely expected while analysts believe Germany is more likely to cut rates given the general weakness of its economy.
"My expectation is that the Irish pound is going to remain under pressure because sterling still looks very well supported," Jim Power, economist at Bank of Ireland Group Treasury, told Reuters.

"Despite the fact that they didn't hike interest rates yesterday in the UK, the market expectation is they'll do it next time around," Power said, adding that sterling could well test 2.70 marks, pushing the punt back toward 0.9750 sterling and below.
John Beggs, economist at AIB Capital Markets, agrees.

"Sterling and the dollar are not exactly striding ahead. They are making steady progress upward but there is a chance that sterling could break significantly higher and if that's the case, the Irish pound will continue to lose ground against sterling, falling to 97 pence."
Analysts say the punt's weakness against sterling and strength in the ERM grid pose a dilemma for the Irish Central Bank.
The punt, which was at 0.9785 by 1100 GMT on Friday, has lost nearly six percent against sterling in the last six months but has gained over 10 percent on the mark in the same period.

It is perched at the top of the Exchange Rate Mechanism, more than nine percent above the Belgian franc, the weakest currency, causing some concern among analysts that Ireland may not fulfil the Maastricht criteria on currency stability.

Meanwhile, the punt's weakness against sterling, allied to strong credit growth and what is widely expected to be a generous tax-cutting budget on January 22, could pose a threat to Irish inflation, analysts say.

AIB's Beggs notes that one third of Irish imports come from Britain while the punt has also lost ground against the dollar recently which could put upward pressure on the price of oil and other raw materials invoiced in dollars.

"There must be the risk of higher imported inflation from here. The question is whether it will be passed on," he said, noting that investors will keep a very close eye on the release of Irish consumer price data for January next month.
But Power says the bank's room for manoeuvre is limited despite the potential inflationary implications of the punt's drop against sterling.

Supporting the punt against sterling through intervention or higher interest rates would further fuel its strength in Europe, possibly damaging Ireland's chances of participating in Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

"The one thing that prevents the central bank from moving is the whole EMU situation. Hiking interest rates would send out all the wrong signals about Ireland's EMU credentials," Power said. "Even more damaging would be the impact it would have on the Irish pound in the ERM grid. It would just further accentuate the strength that is already there."
